## The SCORE programme {#what-is-score}

::: {.small}
- DARPA-funded programme to gauge the credibility of social-science claims
- A stratified sample of papers from **62 journals**, published **2009–2018**
- The central claim of each paper traced from the abstract to the statistic that supports it
- Thousands of researchers, and three repetition studies built on the same sampling frame
:::

::: notes
The three papers that we look at next come from one programme, SCORE, short for Systematizing Confidence in Open Research and Evidence. It was funded, perhaps surprisingly, by DARPA, the research agency of the United States Department of Defense, which wanted to know whether one could predict which findings hold up. It starts from a stratified sample of papers from sixty-two journals, published between 2009 and 2018, and traces the central claim of each paper from the abstract to the statistic that supports it. Three studies then took that sampling frame and each asked one of our three questions, so that the numbers that follow describe one body of literature, asked three different things.
:::

## Reproducibility – Miske et al.

::: {.small}
- **600 papers** sampled (62 journals, 2009–2018)
- Ask the authors for data and code, then try to rerun the reported result
- How often is that even possible?
:::

::: {.src}
@MiskeEtAl2026InvestigatingReproducibilitySocial.
:::

::: notes
Reproducibility is the gentlest of the three tests. The SCORE reproducibility study took six hundred papers, asked the authors for their data and code, and tried to recompute the central reported result from the same data with the same analysis. Its first finding concerns how rarely such an attempt can even start.
:::

## Reproducibility results – Miske et al. {#most-papers-never-reach-the-starting-line}

```{r}
#| label: miske-waterfall
#| fig-width: 8.5
#| fig-height: 3.6
# Published counts from Miske et al. (2026, abstract): 600 papers sampled; the
# authors supplied data for 144 (24.0%); source data rebuilt 38 more, making
# 182 datasets in hand; 143 of those 182 were assessed.
mw <- tibble::tribble(
  ~stage,                 ~n,
  "Sampled",              600,
  "Author data\n(24.0%)",   144,
  "In hand\n(+38 rebuilt)",  182,
  "Assessed",             143
)
mw <- mw |> dplyr::mutate(stage = factor(stage, levels = stage))
ggplot2::ggplot(mw, ggplot2::aes(stage, n, fill = stage)) +
  ggplot2::geom_col(width = 0.65) +
  ggplot2::geom_text(ggplot2::aes(label = n), vjust = -0.4, fontface = "bold",
            colour = ncl_blue, size = 6) +
  ggplot2::scale_fill_manual(values = c(ncl_blue, orange, grey_mid, green)) +
  ggplot2::ylim(0, 660) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = NULL, y = "papers") +
  theme_slide(16)
```

::: {.small}
- Of the **143 assessed**: **53.6%** reproduced precisely, **73.5%** at least approximately
- Counting the unassessable, only about **18%** reproduce
:::

::: {.src}
@MiskeEtAl2026InvestigatingReproducibilitySocial. Published counts: the 143 assessed papers come from 182 datasets, 38 of them rebuilt from source data.
:::

::: notes
The chart reads from left to right. Six hundred papers were sampled, and data were available for twenty-four per cent of them, while for nearly three quarters there was neither data nor code. The team rebuilt thirty-eight more datasets from source data, which made a hundred and eighty-two, and assessed a hundred and forty-three papers. Of those, just over half reproduce precisely and about three quarters at least approximately. The rate sounds respectable until the papers that nobody could check are counted as failures, and then it falls to roughly eighteen per cent, with most of the loss at the first step, obtaining the data.
:::

## Data availability – Miske et al. {#why-some-fields-do-better}

::: {.small}
- Journals with a sharing policy: **66.2–100%** data availability vs **16.0%** without
- By discipline: **54.1%** data availability in political science vs **2.9%** in education
- With data *and* code: **90.9%** approximately reproducible vs **38.1%** from rebuilt source data
:::

::: {.claimcard}
"The most substantial barrier … was the unavailability of author data."

"Reproducibility success does not mean that the finding is correct."
:::

::: {.src}
@MiskeEtAl2026InvestigatingReproducibilitySocial.
:::

::: notes
Access follows policy. In journals with a policy on data sharing, availability runs from about two thirds to all papers, depending on the policy, against sixteen per cent in journals without one, and by discipline political science leads while education trails far behind. The first quotation is the conclusion of the paper, that the most substantial barrier was the unavailability of the data held by the authors. The second, "Reproducibility success does not mean that the finding is correct", says that a reproduced number shows the computation to be faithful and leaves open whether the claim about the world is true.
:::

## Robustness – Aczel et al. {#robustness-aczel-et-al.}

::: {.small}
- **100 studies**, each re-analysed by **≥5 independent analysts**
- The same data for every analyst, each free to choose any *justifiable* analysis
- A peer panel judges whether each pipeline is appropriate
- I was one of its analysts
:::

::: {.src}
The SCORE robustness study [@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness].
:::

::: notes
The middle paper is the study in which I took part. For each of a hundred studies, at least five analysts worked independently, each with the same data and the same claim, free to analyse it in any way that they could justify, and a panel of peers later judged whether each analysis was appropriate.
:::

## Robustness results – Aczel et al. {#same-data-five-analysts-different-answers}

::: {.small}
- **34%** of reanalysis effect sizes within ±0.05 *d* of the original (57% within ±0.20)
- **74%** reached the same conclusion, 24% a null or inconclusive one, **2%** the opposite
- Effect sizes shrank: original mean *d* **0.73** → reanalysis **0.49**
- Observational studies came out less robust than experiments: **28%** against **44%** of the reanalyses within ±0.05 *d*
:::

::: {.src}
@AczelEtAl2026InvestigatingAnalyticalRobustness, pp. 136–139.
:::

::: notes
Free, justifiable choices on the same data move the answer a long way. Only about a third of the reanalyses fell within five hundredths of a Cohen's d of the original, and in only five of ninety-five studies did all the analysts come that close. The conclusions held up better than the magnitudes, with three quarters of the reanalyses reaching the original conclusion, but the effect sizes shrank, from a mean d of point seven three to point four nine. Observational studies, the kind of study on which we work today, came out less robust than experiments.
:::

## Replicability – Tyner et al.

::: {.small}
- **274 claims** from 164 papers, tested on **independent data** (newly collected for 128, existing for 146)
- A median statistical power of **99.6%**, a preregistered protocol, and the original authors consulted
- The strictest test: does the effect reappear in data that the original study did not use?
:::

::: {.src}
@TynerEtAl2026InvestigatingReplicabilitySocial.
:::

::: notes
The third paper is the strictest test, because each claim is checked against data that the original study did not use, newly collected for a hundred and twenty-eight claims and existing for the other hundred and forty-six. The two hundred and seventy-four claims were replicated under protocols that were peer reviewed in advance, with the original authors consulted, and with a median statistical power of ninety-nine point six per cent. At that power an effect as large as the original would be very hard to miss, so a failure cannot be put down to a study too small to detect the effect.
:::

## Replicability results – Tyner et al. {#even-success-shrinks}

```{r}
#| label: tyner-shrink
#| fig-width: 7.5
#| fig-height: 3.2
# Median r: original -> replication (Tyner et al. 2026), inline dumbbell.
sh <- tibble::tibble(
  stage = factor(c("Original", "Replication"),
                 levels = c("Original", "Replication")),
  r = c(0.25, 0.10)
)
ggplot2::ggplot(sh, ggplot2::aes(r, y = 1)) +
  ggplot2::geom_line(ggplot2::aes(group = 1), colour = grey_mid, linewidth = 2) +
  ggplot2::geom_point(ggplot2::aes(colour = stage), size = 8) +
  ggplot2::geom_text(ggplot2::aes(label = sprintf("%.2f", r)), vjust = -1.6,
            fontface = "bold", colour = ncl_blue, size = 6) +
  ggplot2::geom_text(ggplot2::aes(label = stage), vjust = 3.2, colour = ncl_blue, size = 5) +
  ggplot2::scale_colour_manual(values = c(ncl_blue, orange)) +
  ggplot2::scale_x_continuous(limits = c(0, 0.3)) +
  ggplot2::labs(x = "median effect size (r)", y = NULL) +
  theme_slide(16) +
  ggplot2::theme(axis.text.y = ggplot2::element_blank(),
        panel.grid.major.y = ggplot2::element_blank())
```

::: {.small}
- **55.1%** of claims replicated by the significance criterion, and effect sizes roughly **halved**
- Thirteen success criteria give anywhere from **29%** to **75%**
:::

::: {.src}
@TynerEtAl2026InvestigatingReplicabilitySocial.
:::

::: notes
The median effect size halves, from point two five in the originals to point one zero in the replications, as correlations, and by the criterion of significance fifty-five per cent of the claims replicate. Whether a claim replicated is, however, not a single question, since the team scored the same studies against thirteen reasonable criteria of success and obtained rates from twenty-nine to seventy-five per cent. As the paper puts it, "Strictly speaking, there is no such thing as exact replication", and "The problem to solve is not unreplicability per se, it is overconfidence."
:::

## The three Rs across SCORE {#the-three-rs-do-not-travel-together}

:::: {.none}
Reproducible ≠ robust ≠ replicable.

::: {.fragment .fadeInUp}
Across SCORE the three are [**essentially uncorrelated**]{.highlight bg-colour="#ffe3b3"} – knowing one barely predicts the others.
:::

::: {.fragment .fadeInUp}
So there is no single number for 'trust'. You have to ask *which* repetition you mean.
:::
::::

::: notes
One would hope that the three properties go together, so that a reproducible finding is more likely to be robust and a robust one more likely to replicate. [advance] Across SCORE, and to my own surprise, they do not: measured on the same body of papers, the three indicators are essentially uncorrelated, so that knowing one tells us almost nothing about the others. [advance] There is therefore no single score of trust for a finding, and the question whether a finding is reliable is incomplete until we say which kind of repetition we mean. The claim that I was handed in the robustness study is the one on which this workshop is built.
:::
